title: Rucho v. Common Cause (2019)
summary: Claims that a congressional map is an unconstitutional partisan gerrymander are political questions that federal courts cannot decide, because the Constitution supplies no judicially discoverable and manageable standard for how much partisan advantage is too much.
notes: Supreme Court of the United States, 2019. Key line: In this rare circumstance, that means our duty is to say 'this is not law.' (Chief Justice Roberts)

sections.Parties: In the North Carolina case, the appellants are the Republican state legislators (Rucho and others) who defended the congressional map that the Republican-controlled General Assembly enacted in 2016; the appellees are Common Cause and North Carolina voters who alleged that the map discriminated against Democrats. In the companion case, Lamone v. Benisek, Maryland election officials defended a map drawn in 2011 by a Democratic legislature under Governor Martin O'Malley, and Republican voters alleged that the map discriminated against them. The plaintiffs in both cases relied on the First Amendment, the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, the Elections Clause and Article I, section 2. The defendants in both cases were the state officials responsible for adopting and administering the challenged maps.
sections.Material Facts: In 2016 the Republican legislators leading North Carolina's redistricting instructed their mapmaker to use political data to draw a map that would elect ten Republicans and three Democrats. One committee co-chair said he drew the map because 'electing Republicans is better than electing Democrats' and because he did not believe an 11-2 map was possible. A Democratic senator objected that Democratic candidates had won more statewide votes as recently as 2012. The plan passed on a party-line vote. Republicans won 10 of 13 seats in 2016 and 9 of 12 in 2018, with the thirteenth rerun after fraud allegations. In Maryland, Governor O'Malley led a 2011 redistricting, advised by Congressman Steny Hoyer, a self-described 'serial gerrymanderer,' with the stated aim of flipping one district to produce a 7-1 Democratic delegation. That map passed on a party-line vote, flipped the Sixth District in 2012, and a Democrat has held the seat since.
sections.Procedural History: Voters and organizations in each State sued the responsible state officials in federal district court. The district courts in North Carolina and Maryland both held the partisan gerrymandering claims justiciable and ruled for the plaintiffs, finding the maps unconstitutional under theories that included the Equal Protection Clause, a three-part First Amendment test (intent to burden voters by party or voting history, an actual burden on speech or association, and causation) and, in North Carolina, the republican-government principle the court located in Article I, section 2. The defendants appealed directly to the Supreme Court, which heard Rucho v. Common Cause and Lamone v. Benisek together. The Supreme Court held that the claims present nonjusticiable political questions, so the lower courts had no authority to decide them.
sections.Issue: Are claims that a State's congressional districting map is an unconstitutional partisan gerrymander justiciable in federal court? That is, can courts identify a standard that is grounded in a limited and precise rationale and is clear, manageable and politically neutral for deciding when partisan advantage in districting has gone too far, or does Article III's limit of federal courts to cases and controversies of a judiciary nature bar them from answering 'how much is too much' when the Constitution names no baseline of electoral fairness and assigns districting to state legislatures checked by Congress?
sections.Holding: No. Partisan gerrymandering claims present political questions beyond the reach of the federal courts. The Constitution does not require proportional representation, supplies no objective measure of a party's fair share of seats, and offers no standard for deciding how much partisan advantage is too much. Every proposed test fails: the district courts' intent-and-effects standard, the First Amendment viewpoint-discrimination theory, the dissent's median-map baseline built from a State's own districting criteria, and the Article I, section 2 theory, which sounds in the nonjusticiable Guarantee Clause. Remedies for excessive partisanship lie with state constitutions and state courts, independent commissions, and Congress under the Elections Clause. Federal judges have no license to reallocate political power between the two major parties.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts reasoned from the text and structure of Article III and the Elections Clause, read through history. Article III limits courts to questions 'of a Judiciary Nature,' and Baker v. Carr treats questions lacking judicially manageable standards as political questions. The Framers knew gerrymandering, from Patrick Henry's effort against Madison to Elbridge Gerry's 1812 salamander district, and assigned districting to state legislatures with Congress empowered to 'make or alter' the rules, as it did in the Apportionment Act of 1842. The Founders never required proportional representation; Alabama Whigs won 43 percent of the vote in 1840 and no seats. Every proposed test reduces to a political judgment about fairness, which could mean competitive districts, proportional safe seats or traditional criteria, each with partisan effects. Even after choosing a definition a court must answer 'how much is too much,' and the dissent's reply, 'this much is too much,' is not a standard. One-person, one-vote and racial gerrymandering cases differ because arithmetic and the elimination of a racial classification supply a rule. Justice Kagan's dissent began from the constitutional harm: packing and cracking dilute votes in violation of equal protection and the First Amendment, and lower courts had converged on an ordinary test of predominant purpose, substantial effect and no nonpartisan justification, measured against the State's own criteria.

topics.rules-standards: The majority refuses to adjudicate because no rule can say how much partisanship is too much, while the dissent answers that ordinary legal standards of intent, effect and justification are enough.
topics.structure: The Court reads the Elections Clause as assigning districting to state legislatures checked by Congress, a structural allocation that leaves no role for federal courts to apportion political power.
topics.lrs-n-standing-constitutional: The political question doctrine, like standing, flows from Article III's limit of federal courts to cases and controversies 'of a Judiciary Nature.'
topics.lrs-s-accountability: Roberts warns that the unelected and politically unaccountable federal judiciary would assume 'an extraordinary and unprecedented role' if it reallocated political power between the parties.
topics.lrs-k-lawmaking: The majority points to bills introduced in Congress and to state reforms as the proper channel; Kagan replies that bills that never become law are no remedy when the beneficiaries of gerrymanders control the legislature.

learning.separateOpinions: Chief Justice Roberts wrote for a 5 to 4 majority. Justice Kagan dissented, joined by Justices Ginsburg, Breyer and Sotomayor. She argued that the North Carolina and Maryland maps violated the Equal Protection Clause and the First Amendment, that the lower courts' intent, effects and causation test was 'utterly ordinary' and manageable (the North Carolina map was more skewed than all of 3,000 computer-generated alternatives), and that the majority's hoped-for remedies from Congress and state legislatures are illusory because the politicians who benefit from gerrymanders will not end them.
learning.why: The case opens the course by marking the line between law and politics: courts act only under a standard grounded in a limited and precise rationale, and where the Constitution supplies no rule the remedy belongs to legislatures and to Congress under the Elections Clause. It also shows the Court reading constitutional text and structure through history and institutional competence rather than through the harm alleged.
